items.title: Midterms Could Shift Focus of Epstein Abuse to Banks’ Role
items.summary: With an eye on retaking control of Congress, Democrats are introducing a bill that would hold banks accountable for their handling of Jeffrey Epstein’s finances.
items.full_text:
Title: Midterms Could Shift Focus of Epstein Abuse to Banks’ Role - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/business/epstein-banks-midterm-elections.html

Published Time: Thu, 15 Oct 2026 14:31:36 GMT

Markdown Content:
Congressional Democrats are poised to turn their sights to the role that Wall Street played in enabling the sexual-abuse crimes of Jeffrey Epstein.

A group of Democratic legislators, with an eye on retaking the House, the Senate or both in elections next month, are set on Thursday to introduce a bill that calls on financial regulators to investigate banks and financial executives who did business with Mr. Epstein and potentially make criminal referrals to federal prosecutors.

Several committees in the House and Senate are also prepared to interview bankers who worked with Mr. Epstein and potentially hold hearings into his financial affairs if Democrats control either chamber, said Democratic staff members who were briefed on the matter but not authorized to discuss it publicly.

Two backers of the new bill, Senator Elizabeth Warren and Representative Robert Garcia, are the top Democrats on the Senate Banking and House Oversight Committees and likely to become chairs if their party prevails.

The bill, the Epstein Wall Street Records Act, would also require four federal financial regulators, including the Federal Reserve, to publicly release any records they have related to Mr. Epstein and his associates.

Until now, the main congressional investigation into Mr. Epstein this year, by the House Oversight Committee, has focused largely on employees or friends of the disgraced financier, who died by suicide in 2019 after his arrest on federal sex-trafficking charges. The committee has focused less on the handful of big banks that managed thousands of wire transfers for Mr. Epstein — money he used to make payments to the hundreds of teenage girls and young women he sexually abused.

The measure, led by Ms. Warren of Massachusetts, has the backing of three other Senate Democrats and 20 Democrats in the House, including Mr. Garcia of California, according to Ms. Warren’s office.

Image

The Epstein Wall Street Records Act, pushed by Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, has the backing of three other Democrats in the Senate and 20 in the House.Credit...Valerie Plesch for The New York Times

The measure, which will be introduced in both the Senate and House, is unlikely to pass this year. The lone Republican to endorse the bill is Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, the House’s most prominent Republican critic of President Trump and a leading proponent of efforts to force the Justice Department to release all of its investigatory files on Mr. Epstein.

Lawsuits brought on behalf of hundreds of Mr. Epstein’s victims claimed that three big banks — JPMorgan Chase, Deutsche Bank and Bank of America — often ignored, in the pursuit of profits, warning signs relating to his activities. Together, those banks agreed to pay more than $437 million to settle those class-action lawsuits.

But only Deutsche Bank has been penalized by a U.S. regulator for providing banking services to Mr. Epstein. In 2020, the bank paid a [$150 million fine](https://www.nytimes.com/2020/07/07/business/jeffrey-epstein-deutsche-bank-settlement.html) to New York bank regulators, partly because of its failure to practice due diligence in monitoring Mr. Epstein’s financial affairs.

A position paper explaining the bill that was shared with The New York Times said Ms. Warren would introduce the measure because federal financial regulators had not committed to conducting any investigation into Mr. Epstein’s financial affairs. It cited [reporting by The New York Times Magazine](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/08/magazine/jeffrey-epstein-jp-morgan.html), congressional inquiries and information shared under the Epstein Files Transparency Act as among the reasons for introducing the legislation. Ms. Warren’s office on Thursday released a copy of a three-paragraph letter it received in June from the Federal Reserve in which the central bank said it took its oversight of the nation’s banks seriously but could not comment further.

“I have spent the last year calling on Donald Trump’s financial regulators to launch investigations into the big banks and executives who may have enabled Jeffrey Epstein’s horrific crimes,” Ms. Warren said.

The new bill builds on some of the work done by Senator Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, who this summer [released a report](https://www.finance.senate.gov/ranking-members-news/wyden-releases-new-report-on-failure-of-wall-street-banks-to-blow-the-whistle-on-jeffrey-epsteins-sex-trafficking-and-money-laundering-schemes) that focused on the failure of Wall Street banks to promptly notify financial regulators of potentially suspicious transactions they had handled for Mr. Epstein. In the report, Mr. Wyden, who is backing Ms. Warren’s bill, called for Congress to stiffen federal anti-money-laundering laws.

items.title: Shook Research Changes Name to Veritant After Forbes Scandal
items.summary: The company, known for its rankings of wealth advisers, sped up a rebranding after its founder acknowledged a secret $6 million payment to the top editor of Forbes.
items.full_text:
Title: Shook Research Changes Name to Veritant After Forbes Scandal - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/business/media/shook-research-veritant-forbes.html

Published Time: Thu, 15 Oct 2026 13:40:53 GMT

Markdown Content:
The financial data firm Shook Research found itself in the headlines this summer after its founder secretly paid $6 million to the top editor of Forbes, one of the company’s key partners.

Major financial firms like Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo [stopped participating](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/25/business/media/forbes-shook-research-payment.html) in the company’s lucrative rankings of wealth advisers for fear of being tarnished by association. Shook Research then suspended the rankings entirely while it conducted a review of its business.

Now, the company is hoping to move on from the turmoil with a new name — Veritant — and a promise to conduct annual audits of its wealth adviser rankings. It will also publish a new charter to emphasize the independence and sanctity of its lists.

“The reality is we needed to take a beat to let the dust settle a little bit,” said Molly Bennard, the company’s chief executive.

“We needed to do that to regain confidence and to get ourselves organized,” she added.

The new name, a neologism derived from veritas (Latin for truth, and the motto of Harvard), was selected after a monthslong process that was originally planned to conclude at the end of the year, Ms. Bennard said. But when the founder’s payment became public in August, the company decided to speed up the rebranding.

Founded more than a decade ago by RJ Shook and his wife, Liz, Shook Research became the Consumer Reports of wealth whisperers, syndicating its influential list on Forbes.com and selling logos, plaques and online profiles that allowed wealth advisers to advertise their spot on the list.

But the business ran aground this summer after [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/12/business/forbes-editor-fired.html) reported that Mr. Shook had paid Randall Lane, the top editor of Forbes, $6 million for services that included help [selling his business](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/24/business/media/forbes-randall-lane-shook.html) to PPC, a private-equity firm, for an undisclosed sum. (Mr. Lane has described the payment as a “gift” and said his failure to disclose it to Forbes was a “serious error in judgment.”) Shook Research canceled its wealth adviser summit in Las Vegas, which was only months away.

The company hired Charles River Associates, an accounting firm, to examine its methodology for any hint of impropriety. None was found, Ms. Bennard said.

Veritant has previewed some of the changes to its rankings for major wealth advisers, who want the company to resume its lists, Ms. Bennard said. The company will continue its partnership with Forbes, with which it shares revenue, scheduling to publish its next list in December. A revived summit for financial advisers is also in the works, with a venue to be determined.

The company is also planning to debut a new system for advisers to submit data so their firms can be considered for rankings, Ms. Bennard said. The new system will organize types of data that proved difficult to categorize in the past — such as the ways firms make difficult decisions — to make the rankings more authoritative.

“It’s a lot of information,” Ms. Bennard said. “But it could be organized in such a better fashion.”

items.title: Tech Stocks Plunge as Doubts Over A.I. Spending Intensify
items.summary: Tech stocks plunged, led by a steep drop in South Korea’s benchmark index, as concerns over soaring A.I. spending and stubborn inflation fueled a sell-off.
items.full_text:
Title: Tech Stocks Plunge as Doubts Over A.I. Spending Intensify - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/business/chip-stocks-technology.html

Published Time: Thu, 15 Oct 2026 14:26:37 GMT

Markdown Content:
[Technology stocks](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/business/stocks-500-index-ai.html) extended their losses on Thursday, dragged down by a sharp decline in semiconductor shares as investors grew concerned about how companies will finance their enormous artificial intelligence spending plans.

The sell-off followed the S&P 500’s steepest daily decline in months on Wednesday, after data showed U.S. [inflation](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/business/economy/inflation-cpi.html) running hotter than economists expected.

South Korea’s benchmark KOSPI tumbled more than 7 percent, its seventh straight daily decline. The market, which has shed about a fifth of its value over that period, has become a bellwether for the A.I. boom. Shares in other major Asian markets fell sharply, European tech shares wobbled in early trading.

### Here is the latest:

*   [Tech stocks are hit hard, again.](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/business/chip-stocks-technology.html#link-13a5d46f)
*   [Bonds yields fall in choppy trading.](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/business/chip-stocks-technology.html#link-7d315b9e)
*   [Oil prices retreat.](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/business/chip-stocks-technology.html#link-202f0206)
*   [Gasoline prices stay high.](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/business/chip-stocks-technology.html#link-723f07f6)
*   [What they are saying: “No intention to leave food on the table” in A.I. race.](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/business/chip-stocks-technology.html#link-6cb7a5af)

## Tech stocks are hit hard, again.

*   In the United States, the tech-heavy Nasdaq was down more than 1 percent when trading began in New York. Shares of CoreWeave, a company that sells computing power to big A.I. companies, extended its losses, down around 7.5 percent at the opening bell, after heavy losses the day before on its stock and bonds.

*   Semiconductor stocks took a beating in Asia. In South Korea, SK Hynix plunged 11 percent and Samsung dropped more than 9 percent. Taiwan’s TSMC slid 4 percent and Japan’s SoftBank, a major investor in artificial intelligence, dropped more than 9 percent.

*   In Europe, chip makers and related companies suffered steep declines, with ASML, Infineon and STMicroelectronics all losing more than 5 percent in early trading.

## Bonds yields fall in choppy trading.

*   Amid significant volatility, the yields on U.S. Treasuries fell precipitously, with the [10-year note](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/business/term-premium-bond-yields.html) trading just below 5.1 percent early on Thursday. After the U.S. [inflation](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/business/prices-inflation-food-airfare-car-rentals.html) report’s release on Wednesday, that yield had briefly jumped above 5.3 percent.

*   Some analysts attributed the fall in yields, which move inversely to prices, to the turmoil in tech stocks, with investors seeking safety in bonds that offer relatively attractive returns. Before the start of the war in Iran, the 10-year Treasury offered a yield of around 4 percent.

*   Traders expect the Federal Reserve to raise the short-term interest rate it controls by a quarter-point in December, but the odds of an increase at the central bank’s meeting this month jumped after the worse-than-expected inflation report. Kevin Warsh, the Fed chairman, will speak at an International Monetary Fund event in Bangkok on Friday. He will be under pressure to explain why holding off on a rate increase this month is appropriate when [price pressures are picking up](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/business/economy/inflation-cpi.html).

## Oil prices retreat.

*   The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, fell 1 percent to about $105 a barrel.

*   West Texas Intermediate crude, the U.S. benchmark, was trading around $96 a barrel, up about 1 percent.

*   The Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway between Iran and Oman, [remains risky for ships to navigate](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/business/saudi-houthi-hormuz-oil.html) eight months into the war. Attacks near the strait have [claimed the lives of at least 25 commercial seafarers](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/business/iran-war-hormuz-sailors-dead-compensation.html). And at more than two dozen have been struck this month alone.

*   Last month more oil flowed through the strait to global markets than at any point in the war, in large part because of a U.S. military effort guiding ships. Initial data indicates those flows [have largely held up this month](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/business/hormuz-oil-tanker-attacks.html).

*   Oil exports through the Red Sea, which had become an alternate route to the Persian Gulf used by Saudi Arabia, have been interrupted by the worsening fighting between Saudi forces and the Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen.

## Gasoline prices stay high.

*   U.S. gas prices remained elevated on Thursday, at a national average of $4.33 a gallon, according to the AAA motor club. The price at the pump has risen 45 percent since the war began.

*   Gas prices don’t move in lock step with crude, usually trailing increases or drops by a few days.

*   The average price of diesel rose 2 cents to $6.32 a gallon on Thursday, up nearly 70 percent since the start of the war. A deal President Trump announced last week to increase Russian fuel exports is aimed at easing diesel prices, but is not clear that Russia could deliver all the fuel promised by the plan. The amount of diesel Russia could supply is [small relative to the shortfall in fuel supplies from the Middle East](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/business/energy-environment/trump-russia-diesel-prices.html), which have been throttled by the fighting in the region.

## What they are saying: “No intention to leave food on the table” in A.I. race.

*   As tech market jitters persist, TSMC, the main chip manufacturer for Nvidia’s A.I. chips, said it had no intentions of slowing down.

*   “We are using multiple levers to do everything we can, whenever we can, as fast as we can to maximize the support to our customers,” C.C. Wei, the company’s chief executive, said after announcing another quarter of blockbuster earnings. “We have no intention to leave food on the table for others.”
